judge_assessment.explanation: I checked every number and every claim independently and the judge is right on all of them. sqrt(9+16)=5 against the split's 7; sqrt(36+64)=10 against 14; sqrt(5+7)=sqrt(12)=3.4641->3.46 against Bo's 4.88 (=sqrt5+sqrt7=4.882); sqrt(50)+sqrt(18)=5sqrt2+3sqrt2=8sqrt2=11.3137->11.31 against Dana's sqrt(68)=8.25; (25+144)^(1/2)=13 against 17; sqrt(x+9)=5 -> x=16, and Jamal's x=4 fails because sqrt(13)=3.6055; sqrt(20^2+21^2)=sqrt(841)=29 ft exactly, against 20+21=41; and item 8 is exactly as the judge describes - (sqrt a + sqrt b)^2 = a + b + 2sqrt(ab), so the split drops the cross term, and sqrt(x+25)=sqrt(x)+5 forces 10sqrt(x)=0, i.e. the single root x=0 on x>=0. Coverage is complete too, which I checked rather than assumed: every printed answer line has a backing entry (item 4's exact 8sqrt2 AND its decimal 11.31 are both entries; item 6 carries the solve and the substitution; item 8 carries a solve for part (b) and a manual entry for part (a)), the seven planted wrong values are declared as traps and print in the key's 'Common wrong answers' block, and the one genuinely open item is the only manual flag - matching final_response.md's claim exactly.

strengths_to_preserve: The sheet proves the same misconception in five different disguises and says so: perfect squares where the split looks safe (items 1-2), decimals where nothing comes out whole so the answer's 'look' cannot rescue you (item 3, Bo's 4.88), the split run BACKWARDS as sqrt(50)+sqrt(18)=sqrt(68) (item 4, Dana), rational-exponent notation (item 5, Kofi's 25^(1/2)+144^(1/2)=17), inside a radical equation (item 6, Jamal), and inside geometry (item 7, the 20-by-21 patio). A student cannot pattern-match their way through it.

Item 5's teaching note earns its place: after correcting Kofi's 17 it observes that 5, 12, 13 is a right triangle, so 'the legs never add to the hypotenuse' is the same fact in geometric form - which then pays off in item 7's patio diagonal, where the key rejects Sam's 41 on size alone before doing any arithmetic.

Item 8 is a properly split open/closed item: part (a) is declared {"type": "manual"} with a full-credit checklist naming the required artifact (the term 2sqrt(ab)), while part (b) is a machine-checked solve - and the key derives (b) FROM (a) ('the two sides can agree only when the cross term vanishes'), so the open reasoning is load-bearing rather than decorative.
case_summary: A clean ACCEPT that survives independent checking on math, coverage and delivery. Eight problems, all values re-derived and correct; four explicit find-and-fix items against the requested minimum of two; seven planted wrong results all declared as machine-tested traps and printed as 'Common wrong answers'; every answer line backed by a verify entry, with item 4 carrying both the exact 8sqrt2 and the 11.31 decimal the stem asks for; and exactly one manual item (8a), correctly described in final_response.md. Study guide try-its all check out (sqrt(9+40)=7, sqrt32+sqrt8=6sqrt2, sqrt(x+5)=6 -> x=31). One cosmetic note, below the bar for an improvement: the Quick Answers bank prints '6. 16, 16' because id 6's solve and its trap-hosting eval both evaluate to 16, so a grader sees a duplicated value for a single answer line. It is harmless - the number is right either way - but a future author should host that trap on the entry that already exists rather than adding a second one.
